input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-471: Professional Communications. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course focuses on developing and improving verbal and written communication skills specific to the discipline of computer science. Topics include the different forms of writing in computer science (books, theses, journal articles, technical reports, manuscripts, etc.), writing styles of computer scientists, document readability and usability, documents for career readiness, effective presentations, teamwork and peer review, research methods, experimentation, documenting mathematics and algorithms, proper formatting of graphs, figures, and tables, and ethical, social, and professional issues facing Computer Scientists. This course is approved as Writing Intensive. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have credit for CSCI-472. This class is restricted to students with at least 4th year standing COMPSCI-BS or COMPSCI-2M Contact Hours: Lecture 3 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: Writing Intensive: Program Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer Regeneration revision 2: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[acm-code-of-ethics]
The ACM Code directs computing professionals to contribute to society and human well-being. Computing professionals should avoid harm. They should be honest and trustworthy. They should be fair and take action not to discriminate. They should respect the work required to produce new ideas and creative works. They should respect privacy. They should honor confidentiality. Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products. They should maintain high standards of professional competence, conduct, and ethical practice. Robust security should be designed and implemented when appropriate. Ethical computing decisions identify stakeholders, foreseeable benefits and harms, uncertainty, alternatives, and obligations.

[acm-research-practice]
Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. It cites prior work and identifies the contribution being reported. Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work. Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion. Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible. Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification. Conflicts and relevant relationships should be disclosed according to publication policy. A research project narrows a question, reviews literature, defines a reproducible method, evaluates results, and communicates for the intended audience.

[rit-csci-471]
This course focuses on developing and improving verbal and written communication skills specific to the discipline of computer science. Topics include the different forms of writing in computer science (books, theses, journal articles, technical reports, manuscripts, etc.), writing styles of computer scientists, document readability and usability, documents for career readiness, effective presentations, teamwork and peer review, research methods, experimentation, documenting mathematics and algorithms, proper formatting of graphs, figures, and tables, and ethical, social, and professional issues facing Computer Scientists. This course is approved as Writing Intensive. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have credit for CSCI-472. This class is restricted to students with at least 4th year standing COMPSCI-BS or COMPSCI-2M Contact Hours: Lecture 3 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: Writing Intensive: Program Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

beats.claim: The ACM Code of Ethics directs computing professionals to contribute to society and human well-being.
beats.example: Developing open-source software that improves accessibility for users with disabilities.
beats.title: Introduction to ACM Ethical Principles
beats.visualDirection: Display a clean slide with the ACM Code of Ethics logo and a bulleted list of the six core principles: avoid harm, be honest and trustworthy, be fair and non-discriminatory, respect intellectual work, respect privacy, and honor high quality

beats.claim: Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence and cites prior work.
beats.example: A paper stating 'Our algorithm reduces latency by 15%' must include a table comparing baseline and experimental results.
beats.title: Distinguishing Claims from Evidence
beats.visualDirection: Show a side-by-side comparison of a vague claim versus a claim supported by a cited table and reference list

beats.claim: Computer science documents must prioritize readability and usability for their intended audience.
beats.example: A technical report uses clear headings, concise paragraphs, and a glossary for non-specialist stakeholders.
beats.title: Document Readability and Usability
beats.visualDirection: Provide a before-and-after layout of a dense paragraph versus a structured document with headings, bullet points, and a glossary

beats.claim: Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work and ensure reproducibility.
beats.example: A lab manual includes exact software versions, hardware specs, and step-by-step instructions for running experiments.
beats.title: Research Methods and Reproducibility
beats.visualDirection: Display a checklist template for documenting research methods, including version control, environment setup, and data collection steps

beats.claim: Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion.
beats.example: A graph includes error bars and a confidence interval to show the variability of experimental outcomes.
beats.title: Accurate Results Reporting
beats.visualDirection: Show a line graph with properly labeled axes, error bars, and a legend explaining the statistical significance

beats.claim: Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible to maintain research integrity.
beats.example: A thesis section explicitly states sample size constraints and potential biases in user testing.
beats.title: Limitations and Threats to Validity
beats.visualDirection: Create a template slide with a 'Limitations' section containing placeholders for methodological constraints and alternative explanations

beats.claim: Proper formatting of graphs, figures, and tables ensures clarity and professional presentation.
beats.example: A table uses consistent column alignment, clear headers, and units for every numerical value.
beats.title: Formatting Graphs, Figures, and Tables
beats.visualDirection: Display a professionally formatted table with aligned columns, units, and a caption above the table

beats.claim: Teamwork and peer review are essential for improving document quality and catching errors.
beats.example: A group uses a structured peer review form to check for logical gaps, citation accuracy, and clarity.
beats.title: Teamwork and Peer Review
beats.visualDirection: Show a peer review checklist template with categories like structure, clarity, citations, and formatting

beats.claim: Ethical computing decisions identify stakeholders, foreseeable benefits and harms, uncertainty, alternatives, and obligations.
beats.example: A team evaluates a new AI tool by mapping affected users, potential biases, data privacy risks, and alternative approaches.
beats.title: Ethical Decision-Making Framework
beats.visualDirection: Provide a stakeholder analysis matrix template with columns for stakeholder, benefits, harms, uncertainty, and obligations

beats.claim: Students will apply a comprehensive checklist to evaluate technical documents for ethical, methodological, and communicative standards.
beats.example: A final assignment requires students to audit a sample research paper using the checklist to verify claims, methods, formatting, and ethical compliance.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Display a consolidated checklist combining ethical principles, research integrity, document formatting, and peer review criteria

learningObjectives: Students will define the core ethical principles outlined in the ACM Code of Ethics.
Students will identify stakeholder analysis as a method for evaluating ethical computing decisions.
Students will apply ethical decision-making frameworks to real-world technical scenarios.
